source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) Cognitive conflict and restructuring: neural basis of two core components of insight
finding: fMRI with magic tricks. An incongruent cue (new information that contradicts the first representation) raised solution rates versus a congruent cue that fits the first representation. Conflict raised activity mainly in posterior visual and attention areas, not mainly in ACC.
numbers: N=30 analysed (2 more excluded because they already knew most solutions). 20 tricks, 600 observations, 572 valid (285 incongruent, 287 congruent). Solved 59% incongruent vs 26% congruent, F(1,570)=58.81, d=0.64. Cue rated helpful 72% vs 26%, d=0.87. Overall 42.3% correct, 28.7% wrong, 29.0% no answer.
limits: One study, young students, no timing of the Aha moment itself; authors say ACC may fire only at the instant of conflict detection or insight, which their block design missed.
agent_relevance: Strong behavioural evidence that a contradicting cue is what lets a stuck solver change view. For S6: the trigger should be new contradicting information, not time spent stuck.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) congruent cue as lock-in
finding: Congruent cues (which agree with the false representation) gave low solve rates and no distinct brain activity. Agreeing evidence adds nothing and may entrench the wrong view.
numbers: Congruent solve rate 26% vs 59% incongruent; no region more active for congruent than incongruent cues; no region more active for incorrect than correct trials.
limits: Congruent cues were designed to be unhelpful, so this shows lock-in is possible, not that it is typical.
agent_relevance: A retry that only re-reads the same plan or gets agreeing samples is not a conflict signal (matches G4: samples from one model are not independent).

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) restructuring contrast
finding: Correct vs incorrect trials (restructuring) recruited a widespread frontal, parietal, thalamic and basal ganglia network, more frontal than conflict did. Early visual areas dropped out and higher visual and parietal areas took over.
numbers: Cluster-level FWE p<0.05, voxel p<0.001. Trials solved before the cue were excluded from the contrast. Overlap with conflict: frontal eye fields extending to DLPFC, and middle temporal gyrus, both sides.
limits: Correct-minus-incorrect confounds restructuring with success, effort and reporting. Group-level maps only.
agent_relevance: Detecting conflict and rebuilding the representation are two separable steps. Our S6 trigger and O6 reframe should stay separate.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) review of earlier fMRI insight work
finding: Earlier insight fMRI studies gave heterogeneous areas; ACC was the most consistent, right anterior STG for some verbal tasks. The right-hemisphere claim is disputed.
numbers: Cites Dietrich & Kanso review: ACC consistently found; no clear general picture across studies.
limits: Authors' summary of others; different tasks (riddles, remote associates, puzzles) are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: The neural claim 'ACC = conflict = insight' is not solid. Use the behavioural side (contradiction then restructuring), not the brain map.

source: Luo, Niki & Phillips (2004) 'Aha!' effects in a guessing riddle task: an ERP study
finding: Chinese riddles: an answer that broke the solver's initial set gave a more negative ERP at 250-500 ms (N380, peak 380 ms, Cz) than an answer that fit the first thought. Dipole source in ACC. Authors read it as an N2-like conflict signal that marks breaking a mental set.
numbers: 14 subjects, 120 riddles (half difficult, half easy). Aha minus no-aha difference wave max at Cz, latency 380 ms. The P300 window (500-800 ms) showed no Aha effect.
quote: N380 therefore is probably an N2 component and embodies cognitive conflict in breaking a mental set.
limits: Tiny N. Hard-vs-easy riddle is confounded with set-breaking and with surprise. Source localisation from scalp EEG is coarse. Authors say N380 'probably' is an N2.
agent_relevance: Early direct support for the idea that conflict with the first idea shows within about 0.4 s of seeing a contradicting answer. Supports a cheap, code-checked conflict test on the output.

source: Qin, Anderson et al. (2009) Lateral inferior prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex are engaged at different stages in the solution of insight problems
finding: Rival account. In remote-associate and word-fragment puzzles, ACC rose when a solution was retrieved (processing it, subgoal setting), not while the solver was stuck. LIPFC tracked retrieval effort and stopped when the answer arrived. Fits an ACT-R model.
numbers: Experiment 1: 20 right-handed adults (11 women, ages 18-32), 30 s per remote-associate item. Experiment 2 fit by an information-processing model; LIPFC = retrieval, ACC = subgoal setting.
limits: Word puzzles with retrieval, so not the same as impasse over a wrong frame. Authors note LIPFC may instead reflect selection among alternatives.
agent_relevance: The ACC may signal 'a candidate appeared and must be handled' rather than 'conflict'. Do not build S6 on one brain-region story; build it on observable output-versus-expectation mismatch.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Matchstick arithmetic: difficulty follows how many and how strong the constraints that must be relaxed, and how tight the perceptual chunk that must be split. One exposure to a hard type made later hard items as easy as the easiest type.
numbers: Exp 1A N=20, 5 min limit. Median solution time Block 1: Type A 40 s, B 155 s, C 300 s, D 140 s. A<B p<.001; B<C p<.05; A<D p<.001. Block effect F(1,19)=14.41, p<.01. Exp 1B N=38; Exp 2 N=78 (American students) tested similarity of numerals.
limits: Matchstick symbols only; small samples; German and US students. Type D transfer was not significant for solution frequency (p=.13) but was for time (p<.05).
agent_relevance: Names two concrete things a restructure must do: loosen a rule the solver assumed, or split a unit the solver treated as atomic. Operators for O6 can be written as those two moves.

source: Knoblich et al. (1999) transfer after impasse is strong and size-independent
finding: After one solved problem of a type, the same type was solved easily; similarity of the numerals did not change this. What transfers is the relaxed constraint, not surface features.
numbers: Exp 1A: transfer significant for Types B (T=14, p<.001), C (T=23, p<.01), D (T=32, p<.05) by Wilcoxon on times; none for Type A (p=.80). Exp 2: similarity had no measurable effect.
limits: Short delay between blocks within one session; no long-term retention data.
agent_relevance: Store a 'this assumption was wrong' lesson from a solved impasse and reuse it on same-type tasks.

source: Knoblich et al. (1999) two sources of difficulty are separable
finding: Tight chunk (Type D) added difficulty on top of constraint scope: Type D was about as hard as Type B and much harder than Type A, though both need little constraint change.
numbers: Exp 1A medians: A 40 s vs D 140 s, Wilcoxon T=10, N=20, p<.001.
limits: No interval scale to compare the two sources, so only ordering was predicted.
agent_relevance: Impasse can come from a wrongly fused unit (a chunk) or a wrongly assumed rule; the reframe step should ask both questions.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov & Ardislamov (2025) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra
finding: Conceptual extended replication of the claim that handling physical sticks raises matchstick solve rates. It failed: providing an interactive condition did not produce interactive solutions. Movement did not help chunk decomposition and hurt relaxation of high-level constraints.
numbers: Three experimental series (Exp 1: 2 conditions; Exp 2: 4 conditions; Exp 3: 3 conditions in VR); Bayesian regression with ROPE of +/-0.2 log-odds. Total solver movements stayed low in all series.
quote: merely rendering a condition interactive does not instantaneously translate to an increase in the number of movements or a higher success rate
limits: Exact success rates are in Tables 4-6, which I did not extract. Matchstick problems only.
agent_relevance: External action on the problem is not an automatic restructuring aid. Match the aid to the source of difficulty (chunk vs constraint).

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without oracle labels, asking GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2 to review and fix their own answer lowers accuracy. The model cannot tell which of its answers conflict with reality.
quote: after self-correction, the accuracies of all models drop across all benchmarks
limits: Plain 'review your answer' prompts; 2023-era models; reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Self-judged conflict is a poor trigger. G1/G2 hold: revise only from an external, code-located failure.

source: Huang et al. (2024) direction of answer changes and oracle inflation
finding: With an oracle label deciding when to stop, self-correction looks strong, which inflates earlier claims. Without it, models flip right answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; among changes, correct-to-incorrect exceeded incorrect-to-correct. GPT-4-Turbo: GSM8K 91.5 / 88.0 / 90.0, CSQA 84.0 / 81.5 / 83.0. Llama-2: GSM8K 62.0 / 43.5 / 36.5, CSQA 64.0 / 37.5 / 36.5. Three feedback prompts tried; none gave a gain.
limits: Oracle setting is shown only to explain why prior papers reported gains.
agent_relevance: Any scaffold test of S6 must report results with no oracle in the stop rule.

source: Huang et al. (2024) why CommonSenseQA drops most
finding: False options in CommonSenseQA look somewhat relevant, so a review prompt pushes the model to switch to another option. A review prompt itself creates pressure to change.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo were more likely to keep their first answer.
limits: Explanation is the authors' hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Asking for review is not neutral: it biases toward change. Keep review prompts neutral and let code decide whether to adopt a change.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at locating the step where their own chain of thought went wrong, but fix it well when told where. The bottleneck is detecting the conflict, not repairing it.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces, five tasks; 300 per task, 85% wrong-answer and 15% correct traces. GPT-4 best at 52.87 overall mistake-finding accuracy with direct step prompting. Backtracking with true location: wrong-answer traces +18.04 to +43.92 points, correct-answer traces 0 to -11.43. Random location: +5.16 to +21.57 and -6.67 to -15.91.
limits: PaLM-2-generated traces; synthetic tasks (word sorting, shuffled objects, logical deduction, arithmetic, Dyck). Locations come from human annotation.
agent_relevance: Code-found failing step plus model repair is the right split (matches G2). Random-location backtracking still gains but costs correct answers.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompting and plain fine-tuning (STaR, Pair-SFT) give near-zero or negative self-correction. Two-stage multi-turn RL gave the first clearly positive intrinsic gain, mainly by cutting needless flips of right answers.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash on MATH500: base 52.6% to 41.4% (-11.2); Self-Refine 52.8 to 51.8 (-1.0); STaR 53.6 to 54.0 (+0.4); Pair-SFT 52.4 to 54.2 (+1.8); SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4 (+4.4). Wrong-to-right 14.5% vs 9.5% for base; right-to-wrong 15.8% (base) to 1.4%. HumanEval gain 9.1 points.
limits: Needs RL training, not a scaffold. One model family; binary ground-truth rewards.
agent_relevance: Even trained models gain only a few points. A scaffold that blocks needless flips (code decides) is the cheap analogue.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: Survey: no prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from a prompted LLM, except on tasks suited to it. It works with reliable external feedback and after large-scale fine-tuning. Many positive reports use unrealistic settings.
numbers: Three findings: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside special tasks; (2) works with reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Game of 24 style verifiable tasks count as favourable.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey up to 2024; misses 2025 reasoning-model results.
agent_relevance: Confirms G2 and G5: the conflict signal should come from a verifier or tool, not from the model reading its own text.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) realistic vs unrealistic settings
finding: Positive self-correction results usually rely on an oracle stop signal, extra external information, or a weak initial answer. Under fair settings gains vanish unless fine-tuned or externally checked.
numbers: Table 1 marks unrealistic studies in grey; generate-and-rank on Game of 24 treated as equal to having an external verifier.
limits: Classification is the authors' judgement.
agent_relevance: Report any S6 test with the exact verifier used, and compare with a no-verifier arm.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Spontaneous mid-trace changes of approach ('Aha' shifts) in RL-trained reasoning models are rare and linked to lower accuracy. Formal Aha events, which need a gain at the pivot, are vanishingly rare.
numbers: Shifts about 6.31% of traces pooled (about 7.6% for Qwen2.5-1.5B). Accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for unshifted traces, N=723,200. Formal Aha detector fired on 1.79% of samples. At T=0.7, average marginal effect of a shift: -0.0311 (Xwords), -0.0615 (Math); Rush Hour shifts 11.4% of traces with no effect. Same conclusion with formal, GPT-based and lexical detectors.
limits: Small models (Qwen2.5-1.5B main; 7B and Llama 3.1-8B at 500 steps); three domains (cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, Rush Hour); shifts labelled by an LLM judge. External check: DeepSeek-R1 shift rate 0.00-0.25%, GPT-4o 0.88-2.21%.
agent_relevance: The 'Aha moment' in RL reasoning traces does not do the work people assume. Do not count on the model to restructure on its own.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) forced reconsideration under high entropy
finding: Externally triggering a reconsideration cue raised accuracy where spontaneous shifts did not. The gain was large in Math and tiny in crosswords. An entropy gate (top 20% uncertain) was used to split cases.
numbers: Paired Pass 1 vs Pass 2 with an appended cue such as 'Wait, something is not right, we need to reconsider'. Math: 0.3221 to 0.4062, +8.41 pp, N=320,000 pairs; Xwords: 0.0970 to 0.1015, +0.45 pp, N=83,200; Rush Hour +0.01 pp. Math pairs won by Pass 2: 50,574, by Pass 1: 23,500.
limits: Pass 2 is a second sample, so part of the gain may be extra compute, not insight. Spontaneous shifts stayed harmful even in the high-entropy stratum for Math (raw -7.40 pp). Small trained models.
agent_relevance: A code-fired cue helps; model-initiated doubt does not. Candidate S6 trigger (entropy or disagreement) to test against a plain second sample without the cue.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) training does not make shifts useful
finding: Accuracy rose with RL training, but shifted traces did not become more accurate at later checkpoints.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B Xwords 7.69 to 10.00 (+2.31), Math 31.00 to 35.00 (+4.00) at step 950; Llama 3.1-8B Math 61.60 to 66.40 (+4.80) at step 500. No evidence shifts turn beneficial later in training at T=0.7.
limits: Short RL runs on small models.
agent_relevance: Gains from RL did not come from learned insight-like reconsideration.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: The same injected error is corrected when attributed to the user and missed when attributed to the model. The skill exists but is not activated for the model's own text. Appending 'Wait' reduced the blind spot sharply.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%; 62.8% on BIG-Bench Mistake tasks; Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. 5,306 error-correction traces cut it by 76.0%; appending 'Wait' cut it by 89.3%.
limits: Injected errors (with a natural-error check). Closed models tested on a smaller scale.
agent_relevance: Re-attribute the draft to someone else when checking it (fits G5), and test a code-inserted 'Wait' cue.

source: Tsui (2026) cause is training data, not capability
finding: Authors trace the blind spot to post-training data that lacks error-correction sequences, plus a conversational-role direction in activation space that gates correction.
numbers: Fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces: blind spot down 76.0%. 'Wait' appended: down 89.3%, via a nearly independent pathway.
limits: Mechanistic claim comes from the paper's own probes; not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt-side cue can be code-inserted; compare with the +8.41 pp cue effect in the Illusion of Insight paper.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) cue design needed pilots
finding: Tricks were chosen for low spontaneous solving (below 13% after one viewing, mean 2.9%, in an unrelated 70-person dataset) and at least 25% solving after an incongruent cue.
numbers: Two pilot studies; each trick shown with an incongruent cue in 50% of cases across participants.
limits: Cue effect is trick-specific; results depend on cue craft.
agent_relevance: Conflict triggers need specific contradicting information, not a generic 'try again'.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) future methods and limits
finding: Authors propose eye tracking and pupillometry to time the instant of conflict or insight without a motor response. They did not time the Aha moment.
numbers: Frontal eye fields were active for conflict and restructuring.
limits: Proposal only.
agent_relevance: Marks a measurement gap: no timed conflict point in humans.

source: Luo, Niki & Phillips (2004) 'Aha!' effects in a guessing riddle task: an ERP study
finding: Design of the conflict contrast: a hard riddle followed by a keyword that broke the initial reading, versus an easy riddle followed by a keyword that fit it. Prior fMRI work by Luo and Niki (2003) had linked insight to ACC, which motivated the ERP test.
numbers: 120 Chinese riddles, 14 subjects, high-density ERP; N380 measured at Fz, Cz, Pz in the 250-500 ms window.
limits: The contrast mixes difficulty, surprise and set-breaking. No test that separates conflict from error detection or novelty.
agent_relevance: Output-vs-expectation mismatch is the operational definition; code can compute it as a mismatch between a predicted and an actual result.
